contexts.evidence: Section 3, pp. 4192–4193, models attention as a layered graph, corrects for residual connections, and defines matrix-product rollout and capacity-constrained max-flow attention.
Section 3, pp. 4192–4193, models attention as a layered graph, corrects for residual connections, and defines matrix-product rollout and capacity-constrained max-flow attention.

Section 3, pp. 4192–4193: rollout sums products of path weights (matrix multiplication), whereas flow treats attention as capacities, uses bottleneck path values, and avoids shared-edge overflows. The max-flow construction is not the probability mass deposited by the same random walk.
contexts.proposed_replacement: Both commit to a routing-graph view: rollout treats residual-corrected attention matrices as transition kernels of a walk on tokens, whereas attention flow treats their entries as edge capacities and computes maximum flow to each input token.

contexts.evidence: Section 3, pp. 4192–4193, models attention as a layered graph, corrects for residual connections, and defines matrix-product rollout and capacity-constrained max-flow attention.

notes: The final critique that attention weights omit value magnitudes and projection sign is consistent with the defined algorithms; it is a mathematical inference from those definitions, not an experimental result established by this paper.
